Header:
Date: 2026-06-18
Start: 15:00 UTC
Duration: 58 mins
Attendees: Sara Kim (Redwood AE), Daniel Park (Redwood SE), Maya Singh (Vertex CTO), Liam O'Connor (Vertex SRE), Priya Patel (Eng Lead), Ethan Zhao (ML Eng)

Summary (auto): quick walkthrough of autoscaling and capacity planning. talk about reserved capacity, burst policy, queueing/backpressure, kv cache and batching.

[00:00] Sara Kim: hey everyone, thanks for joining, i think we have about an hour, we'll do a deep dive on autoscaling and capacity planning for the workloads you shared, hi maya, liam, priya uh and ethan.
[00:20] Maya Singh: hi, thanks sara. excited. we have a mix of low-latency chat requests and heavy batch embedding jobs overnight so we want to understand how redwood handles spikes and long tail.
[00:30] Daniel Park: great, quick note on attendees, i'll drive the technical bits, sara will cover commercial/next steps. i'll start with an overview of our autoscaler and the assumptions.
[00:45] Daniel Park: our model is hybrid: reserved pools for your baseline throughput, plus a burst tier that can borrow capacity across AZs for short spikes. we emphasize warm pools to mitigate cold-starts, and we use queueing + backpressure before we spin more GPUs to avoid thrash.
[01:10] Priya Patel: can you explain the queueing model - like if we get a sudden 10x qps burst, what happens to p95 latency and do requests queue indefinitely?
[01:25] Daniel Park: good question. by default requests queue up briefly in a front-door queue with dynamic timeouts. we measure token-level latency and have p50/p95 p99 SLOs. for short bursts we drain the queue via burst capacity, typical behaviour: small spikes are absorbed by batching and existing KV caches; medium spikes trigger warm pool redirections; only sustained high traffic triggers spin-up of reserved pools. queueing has a bounded TTL - we prefer failing fast with a 429 rather than huge tail latency.
[01:55] Liam O'Connor: so where do we configure the TTL and backpressure thresholds? is that per-route?
[02:05] Daniel Park: yes per-route; on the console you set target concurrency, max queue depth, and backpressure thresholds. we default to conservative settings but for your chat flows i'd recommend tighter queue TTL (250-500ms) and a burst policy that allows 20% of reserve capacity to be borrowed for under 60s.
[02:35] Maya Singh: what's the impact on cost if we keep a large warm pool vs spin up on demand? we need predictable billing for the enterprise team.
[02:45] Sara Kim: this is core to why teams choose dedicated vs hosted. warm pools cost more because instances are kept warm (reserved GPUs or kept idle), but they reduce p99 cold start by seconds. we can show a modeled cost vs latency tradeoff in the spreadsheet. for predictable billing you can buy reserved capacity with committed usage and then set a small burst band to absorb spikes.
[03:10] Ethan Zhao: curious about KV cache persistence - if we scale down, do we lose KV cache and cold-start on next warm-up? that has big perf impact on chat recall.
[03:25] Daniel Park: current behavior: we persist KV cache to fast ephemeral storage for warm pools; when an instance is evicted we try to migrate the hot cache to a sibling in the same pool, but full persistence to durable store is optional. for private/on-prem we support cache pinning so you can keep a small subset of hot caches in long-lived nodes. note sometimes transcripts/algs call it "K V cash" in our docs hehe.
[03:55] Priya Patel: you mentioned quantization earlier - what's the latency tradeoff if we use 4-bit quantization for our models?
[04:05] Daniel Park: with 4-bit we typically see 1.6-2.2x throughput improvement depending on kernel coverage and sometimes a small accuracy delta. latency for small requests improves modestly, but batching benefits amplify. main caveat: some ops aren't optimized on all hardware - we run a model characterization to recommend quant profile. we'll include recommended quantization profiles in the benchmark sheet.
[04:35] Maya Singh: for VPC/on-prem we have strict network egress rules and need KMS in our VPC. does that change autoscaler behavior?
[04:45] Sara Kim: Redwood Private supports customer-managed KMS and VPC peering. autoscaling semantics are the same but capacity provisioning can be slower for on-prem because spinup is tied to your infra automation; that's why warm pools are critical for private deployments. we'll note the expected spin-up times in your env.
[05:10] Liam O'Connor: hypothetical: overnight batch jobs saturate GPUs, then morning spike of chat hits - how do you prioritize realtime traffic?
[05:20] Daniel Park: we support route-level prioritization and preemption policies. realtime chat routes can have high priority and will preempt lower-priority batch slots in the burst tier; we also recommend separate dedicated pools for batch vs realtime to avoid noisy neighbor effects.
[05:45] Priya Patel: do you support per-tenant quotas and RBAC to prevent one team from exhausting reserve?
[05:50] Sara Kim: yes, via Console you can set per-team quotas and RBAC. Enterprise includes strict isolation options - dedicate a pool per team or project.
[06:05] Maya Singh: what metrics should we send to you to size reserved GPUs? we have request traces but not token-level histograms.
[06:15] Daniel Park: token-level histogram, sequence length distribution, concurrency per route, and p95 target are most useful. if you can share 2 weeks of traces we'll run a capacity planner and return recommended reserved GPU counts and warm pool sizes.
[06:35] Ethan Zhao: about batching - how do you choose batch windows? we're worried about adding latency to single-turn chat messages.
[06:45] Daniel Park: batching is adaptive: short aggregation windows (2-8ms) for low-latency routes, larger windows for high throughput. for single-turn chat we use micro-batching and dynamic timeouts; you'll see a small ms bump but large throughput wins at scale. you can cap max batch size per route.
[07:10] Liam O'Connor: are there queue metrics we can export to our prometheus? we want to alert on queue depth and tail latency.
[07:20] Daniel Park: yes we export per-route metrics: queue_depth, in_flight_tokens, p50/p95/p99 latency, cold_start_count. we can set up an integration to push to your prometheus/grafana or expose via our tracing hooks.
[07:40] Maya Singh: any case studies or numbers for customers who had similar pattern (overnight batch + morning spikes)?
[07:48] Sara Kim: we'll share two anonymized case studies in the follow-up and the benchmark spreadsheet with simulated traffic we used.
[08:00] Priya Patel: what about backoff strategy on client side, should we do exponential retry or drop? we have mobile clients so UX matters.
[08:10] Daniel Park: best practice is jittered exponential with capped retries and use 429s as signal to degrade gracefully. we provide SDK helpers to surface throttle headers and retry-after so apps can do smarter retries.
[08:30] Ethan Zhao: if we want strict cost control can we limit burst to a hard dollar cap per day?
[08:35] Sara Kim: yes, you can set budget caps and circuit breakers; when budget exceeded we fall back to a cheaper model or return a 429 depending on policy.
[08:50] Maya Singh: for the pilot, can we run a two-week test with a small reserved pool + burst policy, and measure p95 and cost?
[08:58] Sara Kim: absolutely, pilot is the recommended path. we'll size a small reserve for the pilot and instrument metrics.
[09:10] Daniel Park: quick technical note: queueing math we use is an M/M/c style approximation for initial sizing plus trace-driven simulations for tail latencies. we run Monte Carlo with your request traces to recommend warm pool and reserved counts.
[09:35] Priya Patel: are there any gotchas with autoscaler oscillation? we want to avoid scale up/scale down flapping.
[09:45] Daniel Park: yes flapping occurs with naive thresholds. we use hysteresis windows and scale-step limits plus predictive autoscaling using short-term trend forecasts. recommended: 30-90s scale-up smoothing and longer scale-down cooloffs.
[10:05] Liam O'Connor: do you support GPU fractionalization or multi-tenancy on a single GPU for small models to improve utilization?
[10:15] Daniel Park: we support model packing and multi-instance per GPU for smaller models, and that helps utilization but increases complexity around isolation and tail latency. it's configurable per pool.
[10:35] Maya Singh: any security notes for VPC private? auditing, logs, SSO?
[10:40] Sara Kim: yes SOC2, SSO via SAML, audit logs, and KMS integrations. we'll share the security pack in follow-up and can schedule a compliance call if needed.
[10:55] Ethan Zhao: how quickly can you deliver the benchmark spreadsheet with config suggestions?
[11:00] Sara Kim: we can send an initial spreadsheet within 48 hours and a tuned plan after we ingest traces (2-3 business days).
[11:12] Maya Singh: ok sounds good. any other questions from your side?
[11:20] Priya Patel: one more - do you have recommendations for embedding workloads vs chat workloads co-locating on same pool?
[11:30] Daniel Park: generally keep them separate; embeddings are heavy throughput but can be scheduled in batch windows, chat needs low-tails so separate pools or partitioned pool is recommended. if you must co-locate, use strong priority and preemption policies.
[11:50] Sara Kim: recap / next steps: we'll send benchmarks, autoscaler configs, security docs, and propose pilot sizing; maya you will send traces and final success criteria. schedule: sara to email by 2026-06-20.
[12:10] Maya Singh: thanks everyone, appreciate the detail. we'll follow up on traces and schedule the pilot.
[12:18] Sara Kim: thanks all, we'll record action items and close.

End of transcript.
